title: Public or private health insurance in Germany: how to decide
description: Statutory and private health insurance compared for international students and professionals: eligibility, costs, doctor access, family cover and switching rules.
html:
Everyone living in Germany must have health insurance, and for most newcomers the first real decision is which system to join. The statutory system covers about nine in ten residents; the private system is smaller but offers a different deal. Both are accepted for visa and enrolment purposes. Here is how they differ on the points that matter.

1. Who can join which

Statutory insurance is open to nearly everyone: students under 30, employees below a certain income and most family members. Private insurance requires eligibility: students, self-employed people, civil servants and employees above the income threshold can choose it. Some visa types, such as language course visas, are not accepted by the statutory system at all, which makes private cover the only route.

2. What it costs

Statutory student insurance has a fixed rate, currently around €130 a month including long-term care, until age 30. After that the rate rises noticeably. For employees the premium is a percentage of salary, shared with the employer. Private premiums depend on age, health and the level of cover; student plans start around €125 and rise more gently with age. Employees pay the full premium themselves unless the employer contributes.

3. Paying for treatment

With statutory cover you show your insurance card and the doctor bills the insurer directly. With private cover you usually receive an invoice, submit it to the insurer and are reimbursed, though hospitals often bill the insurer directly for larger sums. Private insurers have made this easier with apps that process invoices within days.

4. Access to doctors

Private patients can see any doctor, including practices that only treat private patients, and typically get appointments faster. Statutory patients are limited to doctors who accept statutory patients, which is most of them, but waiting times for specialists can be long in some cities.

5. Hospital and dental benefits

Statutory cover includes hospital treatment in a shared room and basic dental care. Private plans usually include a single or double room, treatment by senior doctors and a higher share of dental costs, including crowns and orthodontics depending on the tariff.

6. Family cover and switching

Statutory insurance covers a non-working spouse and children at no extra cost. Private insurance charges for each family member. Switching is the point most people underestimate: a student who chooses private cover keeps it for the whole of the degree and can only return to the statutory system after graduating or changing status. Choose with the full length of your stay in mind, not just the first year.

The short version

Under 30, planning to stay long-term or bringing family: the statutory system is the safer default. Over 30, healthy, single and keen on faster access: a private student plan is often cheaper and more comfortable.
